traveler: Constantine XI Palaiologos, Emperor and Autocrat of the Romans
title: The Last Emperor of the Romans: from the Morea to the Mesoteichion
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Constantinople, the fourth son is born
stops.date_confidence: The day, 8 February, is firm across the sources; the year is contested between 1404 and 1405 and is left contested. The birthplace within the city is undocumented, and Blachernae, the working imperial residence of the period, is an inference. Sphrantzes's lifespan figure reads 'forty-nine years, three months, and twenty days' in the De Re Militari translation and 49 years, 4 months, 20 days in a second rendering of the same passage; that discrepancy is one of the two levers on the birth year.
stops.campa: A fourth surviving son is born to Manuel II Palaiologos and Helena Dragas on the eighth of February, in a palace on the northern slope of the Sixth Hill, hard against the land walls. The old Great Palace down by the sea is a ruin; the household lives at Blachernae now, where an emperor can hear his own gates being opened. The empire the child enters is a city, a scatter of islands, and a province in the Peloponnese that obeys when it suits it. Three brothers stand ahead of him in the line.
stops.quote: My late emperor, the martyr, lived for forty-nine years, three months, and twenty days.
stops.quote_source: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus, translated excerpt in 'The Siege of Constantinople in 1453 According to George Sphrantzes,' De Re Militari
suggested_refs: The Palace of Blachernae at Ayvansaray, imperial residence of the late Palaiologan house
sources: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (De Re Militari excerpt)

stops.name: Constantinople, the boy left holding the city
stops.date_confidence: The regency ran November 1423 to November 1424, John VIII returning in that month after failing to procure help; the February 1424 peace with Murad II falls inside the regency and does not close it. The dossier's shorter range, ending in February 1424, is corrected here. Day within November not recorded.
stops.campa: John VIII sails west to beg soldiers from Latin princes, and Manuel II is past governing. That leaves a nineteen-year-old in the palace with the seals. Constantine holds the capital for a year, and in February the peace with Murad II is concluded: the city stands, and pays for standing, which is the only statecraft the house has left. His brother comes home the following November having procured no help anywhere, and takes the seals back. The regency has run a full twelve months. Constantine is twenty.
suggested_refs: The February 1424 peace with Murad II, concluded during Constantine's first regency

stops.name: Constantinople, his father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Manuel II Palaiologos dies on the twenty-first of July, having spent his reign travelling Europe as a supplicant and his last years telling his sons that the Turks are best handled by keeping them divided and never by provoking them. John VIII becomes senior emperor. Constantine is twenty-one and has no throne in view. He will keep to his father's advice for twenty-eight years, and abandon it in a single season when there is nothing left to divide. They bury Manuel at the Pantokrator monastery.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Manuel II Palaiologos at the Pantokrator monastery, Constantinople

stops.name: Mesembria, the appanage on the Black Sea
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, month and day not recorded; defaulted to 1 January. The grant is dated to 1425, following Manuel II's death in July of that year.
stops.campa: The new senior emperor pays his brother in towns. Mesembria comes first, a walled peninsula thrust into the Black Sea, forty churches deep in old stone, handed back to the Romans by the Treaty of Gallipoli twenty-two years earlier when the Ottoman house was fighting itself. Constantine takes possession of a port that has changed hands more often than it has changed shape, and that an Ottoman column out of Adrianople can reach in under a week. A narrow sand causeway joins it to the mainland, and the walls stand where the causeway meets the rock.
suggested_refs: The fortified peninsula and churches of Mesembria, modern Nesebar

stops.name: Selymbria, the western end of the grant
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, month and day not recorded; defaulted to 1 January.
stops.campa: Fifty miles west of the capital on the Marmara shore, Selymbria sits on a hill of some fifty-six metres that Michael III built up six centuries before. In the preceding decades it has fallen to the Ottomans and been recovered more than once, which is the whole of its recent history. Eighteen years from now Constantine will hand it to Theodore II in exchange for the Morea, which is what Theodore wants and what he wants himself. For the present it is the western anchor of a lordship whose three pieces do not touch each other.
suggested_refs: The hill fortress of Selymbria, modern Silivri, on the Marmara road to Constantinople

stops.name: Derkos, the third town
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, month and day not recorded; defaulted to 1 January. The identification of Derkos with the Terkos or Durusu lake fortress northwest of Constantinople rests on standard gazetteer usage and could not be re-verified by direct fetch in this pass. Tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The third name in the grant is Derkos, a fortress on the lake behind the Black Sea shore, north and west of the capital. It watches the approach an army coming down from Thrace would use. Nothing about it makes a principality; it makes a picket. The three towns together can be crossed by an Ottoman column inside a week, and the administration of them is the administration of places that exist to give warning. He holds them for two years. In 1427 John VIII sends him south to the Morea.
suggested_refs: The lake fortress of Derkos, modern Durusu, on the Black Sea approaches to Thrace
sources: standard Byzantine-period gazetteer identification of Derkos

stops.name: Mystras, the first arrival in the Morea
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the day after Christmas, Constantine rides into Mystras with John VIII's expedition against Carlo I Tocco. He is twenty-three, and will spend twenty-two of his remaining years on this mountain. The town climbs a spur of Taygetos in tiers: the Despot's Palace, the monasteries, the houses stacked under a Frankish castle the Romans took by treaty a century and a half ago. It is the only part of the empire that still has farmland behind it. Above the last roofs the mountain goes up bare and holds snow into May.
suggested_refs: The Despot's Palace at Mystras, seat of the Despotate of the Morea

stops.name: The Echinades, Tocco's fleet broken
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the dossier's 1428 to 1427: the article names 'the Battle of the Echinades (1427), a naval skirmish off the coast of Glarentza.' Month and day not recorded; defaulted to 1 January. The consequent transfer of Glarentza took place 1 May 1428.
stops.campa: Off the islands at the mouth of the Acheloos, the imperial fleet catches Carlo I Tocco's ships and beats them. It is a skirmish rather than a battle, and it settles more than a battle usually does: Tocco gives up Glarentza and the rest of his holdings in Elis, and offers his niece with them. The empire has not won a naval action worth naming in living memory. This one buys a port, a castle, a wife, and the western half of a peninsula. The terms are agreed within months, and the transfer of Glarentza follows on the first of May, 1428.
suggested_refs: The Echinades islands off the Acheloos mouth, site of the 1427 action against Carlo I Tocco

stops.name: Glarentza, the marriage to Theodora
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected to the Glarentza article's 37 deg 56 min 24 sec N, 21 deg 08 min 14 sec E; the dossier's pin lay about 1.6 km southeast of the medieval site.
stops.campa: Maddalena Tocco is married to Constantine at Glarentza and takes the name Theodora, as a Latin bride entering the Roman house is expected to do. The town around the ceremony is a Frankish foundation with a mint and a harbour, built by the Villehardouin princes of Achaea and now signed over as her dowry. He is proclaimed despot of the Morea about the same date. Two of the three surviving sons of Manuel II now govern the Peloponnese between them, in the name of a third.
suggested_refs: The port and mint of Glarentza, Latin foundation of the Principality of Achaea

stops.name: Chlemoutsi, the castle he campaigns from
stops.date_confidence: The residence is dated to the period 1428-1430 in the sources consulted; no month or day is recorded and the date is defaulted to 1 January 1428 to order the segment.
stops.campa: He moves into Chlemoutsi, the great hexagonal keep the Franks raised on a hill above the Ionian, and makes it his residence and his forward base. From its walls the whole of Elis lies open and Zakynthos sits on the water to the west. Inside, the vaulted galleries are cold enough that the garrison keeps fires through the spring. From here the road runs north and east to Patras, the richest port in the Peloponnese, held by a Latin archbishop who answers to Rome and pays tribute to nobody Constantine recognizes.
suggested_refs: Chlemoutsi castle above Kyllini, thirteenth-century seat of the princes of Achaea

stops.name: Patras, the horse shot under him
stops.date_confidence: Formal siege operations are dated to around 20 March 1429; the lower city surrendered that year. The incident of the horse shot from under Constantine and Sphrantzes's capture while saving him is carried by the timeline but is not narrated by the Patras Castle article, which confirms only that Constantine took control and repaired the walls. The horse incident is therefore reconstruction.
stops.campa: The siege of Patras opens around the twentieth of March. The lower town gives in; the castle on the hill does not. In the fighting Constantine's horse is shot from under him and he goes down among the enemy, and George Sphrantzes, his friend and secretary, gets him out and is taken prisoner doing it. The two of them have known each other since boyhood in the palace, and twenty-four years from now Sphrantzes will write the only sober account of how this man dies. The incident comes down through the timeline of Constantine's life. The account of the castle itself does not mention it.
suggested_refs: The castle of Patras, held by its Latin archbishop until 1430

stops.name: Glarentza, the walls pulled down and the wife buried
stops.date_confidence: Theodora's death is dated November 1429; day not recorded. The Catalan seizure and the demolition of Glarentza's fortifications are dated 1429 by the Glarentza article, which says only that Constantine was forced to ransom the town back and gives no sum: the figure of 6,000 Venetian ducats is not in that page and is not printed here. Theodora was first buried at Glarentza and later translated to Mystras; the receiving church at Mystras is not established in anything reached.
stops.campa: Catalans take Glarentza while the army is at Patras, and Constantine has to buy his own town back before pulling its walls down himself, so that no raider can ever shelter in them again. The mint stops; the harbour empties. It had been the busiest Latin port on the western coast for two hundred years. In November Theodora dies there, a year and four months married, and they bury her in the town he has just dismantled. Later she is moved to Mystras. Which church received her is not known.
suggested_refs: The demolished fortifications of Glarentza, razed on Constantine's own order in 1429

stops.name: Patras, the citadel surrenders
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 July.
stops.campa: In July the castle finally opens its gates, and two centuries of Latin rule over Patras end. Constantine repairs the walls and puts Sphrantzes in as governor of the place his capture helped take. The port is the wealthiest thing the Palaiologoi have acquired by force in generations, and its revenues are the reason the Morea can pay soldiers at all for the next fifteen years. Rome protests the seizure of an archbishop's city. Nothing follows from the protest.
suggested_refs: The walls of Patras, repaired by Constantine after the 1430 surrender

stops.name: Kalavryta, the exchange with Thomas
stops.date_confidence: Month and year carried by the timeline; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 March. Not re-verified by direct fetch in this pass.
stops.campa: The brothers trade provinces the way other men trade fields. Constantine gives Thomas the plain of Elis, with Glarentza's ruins and Chlemoutsi in it, and takes Kalavryta up in the mountains of Achaea. Kalavryta lies closer to Mystras, and Mystras is where he means to end up; the exchange is made with an eye eleven years ahead. The Peloponnese is now split three ways among three sons of Manuel II. Theodore holds Mystras, Thomas the western plain, Constantine the mountains between them.
suggested_refs: The mountain town of Kalavryta in Achaea, taken in exchange for Elis

segments.name: Regent for a Union He Did Not Sign

stops.name: Constantinople, the second regency begins
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the dossier's November 1437: Constantine reached Constantinople on 24 September 1437 to take up the regency, two months before John VIII sailed for Italy on 27 November. The regency ran to February 1440. Nicholas of Cusa's papal delegation was in Constantinople in the same season arranging the Greek passage to the council; no meeting between Cusa and Constantine is attested, and the relation is the policy, not a documented encounter.
stops.campa: Constantine comes up from the Morea in September and takes the capital in charge again, while his brother prepares to sail for Italy and sell the Roman church for an army. The Latin embassy in the harbour that autumn includes Nicholas of Cusa, come to arrange the passage; no meeting between him and Constantine is recorded. Constantine will govern the city for two years and five months, and will have to enforce whatever is agreed in Italy without ever having signed it. John VIII sails on the twenty-seventh of November.
suggested_refs: The papal delegation of 1437 at Constantinople, negotiating the Greek passage to the Council of Ferrara-Florence

stops.name: Constantinople, the decree arrives from Florence
stops.date_confidence: The Union of Florence was proclaimed 6 July 1439. Constantine was regent in Constantinople and was not at the council; the date here is the decree's, not the date of its arrival in the city, which is not recorded. He never personally signed it.
stops.campa: In a cathedral in Tuscany the two churches are declared one, and the delegation that signs does so on behalf of a city that was not asked. The bull is read out in Latin and in Greek. Constantine is in Constantinople, governing the people who will have to live under it, and he puts no name to the document, then or ever. The union is the price agreed for western ships. In the capital the clergy have already begun refusing communion with the men who signed. No western fleet arrives that year, or the next.
suggested_refs: The bull Laetentur Caeli, proclaimed at Florence, 6 July 1439

stops.name: Mytilene, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 August. Sphrantzes had been sent to Lesbos in December 1440 to arrange the match. The detail that Constantine left Caterina temporarily with her family comes from the pool's synthesis of the Sphrantzes-derived chronology and was not re-verified in this pass.
stops.campa: Sphrantzes goes to Lesbos in December to negotiate, and in August Constantine marries Caterina Gattilusio in the castle at Mytilene. Her father Dorino is Genoese, lord of the island by a marriage into the imperial house two generations back, and rich on alum and mastic. She is about seventeen. Constantine is thirty-seven, and marrying a Latin for a fleet and a frontier for the second time. He leaves her with her family and sails for the Morea, meaning to send for her later.
suggested_refs: The Gattilusio castle at Mytilene, Genoese seat on Lesbos

stops.name: Palaiokastron, the blockade off Lemnos
stops.date_confidence: The blockade is dated 1442; month and day not recorded and defaulted to 1 July to precede the August death. Corrected from the dossier, which placed the illness in the waters off Myrina: the Caterina Gattilusio article locates the illness and death at Palaiokastron, on the north of Lemnos. No precise coordinate for Palaiokastron could be established; the pin here is an approximate north-coast position and should be refined.
stops.campa: Demetrios Palaiologos brings an Ottoman army against Constantinople to take his brother's throne, and John VIII sends for Constantine. He puts to sea with Caterina and an Ottoman fleet closes on them at Lemnos, pinning the party at Palaiokastron on the north of the island. The war they were sailing to fight goes on without them, and is decided without them. Caterina is pregnant, and on the beached, blockaded coast of an island neither of them wanted to see, she falls ill.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman naval blockade of Lemnos, summer 1442

stops.name: Myrina, Caterina buried
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 August. Corrected from the dossier's hedge that later sources merely connect the death to pregnancy: Sphrantzes, a contemporary who negotiated the marriage, records that she fell ill and suffered a miscarriage that August. Myrina is the burial place; the death was at Palaiokastron.
stops.campa: She miscarries and dies in August, a year married. Sphrantzes, who arranged the match himself and is writing within living memory of it, sets down the illness and the miscarriage in plain words. They bury her at Myrina under the rock the Genoese fortified, on the west shore facing the sea road home. Constantine is thirty-eight and twice a widower, with no living child by either wife, and the ship that is holding him at anchor is an enemy's. He does not marry again.
suggested_refs: The grave of Caterina Gattilusio at Myrina, Lemnos

stops.name: Constantinople, arriving after it is over
stops.date_confidence: Month and year carried by the timeline; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 November.
stops.campa: He reaches the capital in November, and the crisis he was summoned for has already collapsed on its own. Demetrios and his Ottoman backers have withdrawn. Demetrios is put under guard for a while and then let out again, because the house has too few men in it to spend one. Constantine has lost a wife and an unborn child to a summons that made no difference to anything. His soldiers are in the Morea, and he goes back south to them before the winter closes the roads.
suggested_refs: The brief imprisonment of Demetrios Palaiologos after his Ottoman-backed attempt of 1442

stops.name: Mystras, the despotate in his own hands
stops.date_confidence: Month and year carried by the timeline; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 November. The exchange by which Theodore II left the Morea for Selymbria is dated 1443; the specific terms come from the pool's synthesis of the family rearrangements.
stops.campa: Theodore II has had enough of the Morea and wants a town near the capital, so he takes Selymbria and Constantine takes Mystras. After sixteen years of campaigning in the Peloponnese for other men's account, Constantine now sits in the Despot's Palace itself, ruling with Thomas and outranking him. Below the palace the town runs down the slope in stacked lanes; above it the Frankish castle holds the ridge. He starts, almost at once, on a wall a hundred and thirty miles north.
suggested_refs: The Despot's Palace at Mystras, occupied by Constantine from 1443

The mid-fifteenth-century fresco portrait of Constantine XI at the Holy Monastery of the Taxiarchs, Aigialeia, announced by the Greek Ministry of Culture in December 2024, whose painter officials suggest had seen him at Mystras
sources: Archaeology.org, 'Portrait of Last Byzantine Emperor Discovered in Greece,' 20 December 2024

stops.name: The Hexamilion, the wall raised again
stops.date_confidence: Completion is dated March 1444; day not recorded and defaulted to 1 March. Coordinates corrected to the Hexamilion article's 37 deg 55 min 34 sec N, 22 deg 58 min 21 sec E; the dossier's pin lay about 1.4 km east, out toward the modern canal.
stops.campa: Six miles of wall across the neck of the Peloponnese, first built under Theodosius II, thrown down and raised again more times than anyone bothers to count. Constantine and Thomas rebuild it, and pay for it by squeezing the landowners of the Morea for money and forced labour until the Moreot nobility hates them. By March it stands. On paper the peninsula is now an island. The Ottomans have already come through this line in 1423 and again in 1431, and on both occasions the wall was standing when they arrived.
suggested_refs: The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth, rebuilt 1443-1444

stops.name: Thebes, the last offensive of the Romans
stops.date_confidence: Dated to summer 1444; month and day not recorded and defaulted to 1 July. Corrected from the dossier's chronology, which claimed the capture of Athens as well: Nerio II Acciaioli lost Thebes and was forced into tribute and vassalage but retained the Duchy of Athens itself, and Murad helped him retake Thebes in 1446.
stops.campa: With the Ottoman army committed on the Danube, Constantine crosses the Isthmus and goes north into Boeotia. Thebes falls. Nerio II Acciaioli, Florentine duke of Athens, keeps his duchy but pays his tribute to Constantine instead of to the sultan and does homage for it. Nerio's house had been paying that tribute to the Ottomans since his father's day. No army under the name of the Roman Empire will take ground after this one. In 1446 Murad helps Nerio take Thebes back.
suggested_refs: The Kadmeia of Thebes, taken from Nerio II Acciaioli in 1444

stops.name: Thebes, the news from Varna
stops.date_confidence: The Battle of Varna is firmly dated 10 November 1444. Constantine was not at Varna; he was campaigning in central Greece, and the stop stands where he stood. The refusal of Ottoman demands to withdraw is attested.
stops.campa: On the tenth of November, five hundred miles away on the Black Sea, Murad II destroys the crusading army of Wladyslaw of Poland and Janos Hunyadi, and the king of Hungary is killed on the field. The last coalition Christendom will assemble for this purpose is finished in an afternoon. Word comes south to Boeotia. Constantine keeps campaigning, and when the Ottoman demand arrives that he withdraw behind the Isthmus and give back what he has taken, he refuses it.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Varna, 10 November 1444, and the destruction of the last crusade

stops.name: The Hexamilion, the wall broken with guns
stops.date_confidence: attested. The assault ran from the end of November to the breach of 10 December 1446. The Hexamilion article confirms the December 1446 breach within the sequence of Ottoman assaults in 1423, 1431, 1446 and 1452.
stops.campa: Murad brings artillery to the Isthmus at the end of November and the six miles of wall come apart in days. What follows on the far side is killing and enslavement across the open country, and the brothers get out with their lives and reach Mystras. Constantine accepts the sultan's overlordship, agrees to tribute, and undertakes never to rebuild the wall. The breach is dated the tenth of December. The Hexamilion had been forced twice before within living memory, in 1423 and again in 1431.
suggested_refs: The breach of the Hexamilion by Ottoman artillery, 10 December 1446

stops.name: Mystras, two pieces of news
stops.date_confidence: John VIII died childless at Constantinople on 31 October 1448; Murad II gave his assent to Constantine's succession on 6 December 1448. Constantine was in the Morea for both and is not recorded travelling to the Ottoman court: the business at Adrianople was done by envoys. The stop is dated to the first of the two events and holds both.
stops.campa: John VIII dies childless on the last day of October, and the succession comes down to Constantine and Demetrios, who has twice raised Ottoman troops against the family. Helena Dragas, their mother, settles it from the palace in the capital, and settles it for Constantine. Envoys ride to Adrianople, and on the sixth of December Murad II gives his assent to the choice. The Roman emperor will take his throne by an Ottoman sultan's leave. Constantine is in the Morea throughout, and does not go to Adrianople himself.
suggested_refs: The dynastic arbitration of Helena Dragas, securing Constantine's succession over Demetrios

stops.name: Mystras, invested as emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the proclamation and investiture at Mystras. No patriarch crowned him, and it is unclear whether a formal coronation took place at all; whether the ceremony was in the palace or in a church is not established.
stops.campa: On the feast of the Epiphany they proclaim him emperor at Mystras, in a provincial town six days from his capital. No patriarch is present. Nobody sets a crown on him; the sources cannot even agree that a coronation happened, or whether the ceremony took place in the palace hall or in a church. He is the last man to hold the title and one of the very few to receive it without the rite. Constantine XI, Emperor and Autocrat of the Romans, acclaimed on a hillside in the Peloponnese.
suggested_refs: The Metropolis and the palace hall at Mystras, the two candidate sites of the January 1449 investiture

stops.name: Constantinople, the emperor enters his city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of arrival. The vessel was Catalan. The landing point within the city is not documented.
stops.campa: He comes home on a Catalan ship in March, because the empire has no navy able to carry its emperor to his own capital. Demetrios meets him and acknowledges him in public, because the family requires it of him. The city he has come back to holds perhaps fifty thousand people inside walls built for half a million. Where he stepped ashore is not recorded. The reign runs from here: four years, four months and twenty-four days, by Sphrantzes's count afterwards.
stops.quote: His reign lasted four years, four months, and twenty-four days. He had been the eighth emperor of the Palaeologan Dynasty.
stops.quote_source: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus, translated excerpt in 'The Siege of Constantinople in 1453 According to George Sphrantzes,' De Re Militari
suggested_refs: The silver coinage of Constantine XI, including the half-stavraton first recorded from the hoard published in Revue numismatique, 1991
sources: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (De Re Militari excerpt)
Revue numismatique, 1991, on the Constantine XI hoard (Persee.fr)

stops.name: Constantinople, his mother dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Helena Dragas dies on the twenty-third of March. A Serbian princess, she had come to Constantinople as a bride fifty-eight years earlier, outlived her husband by a quarter of a century, and taken the veil as the nun Hypomone, which means patience. She had decided which of her sons would be emperor and made the decision hold, and there is nobody left who can do that a second time. Constantine is forty-six, unmarried and childless. Demetrios and Thomas are in the Morea, and are not speaking to each other.
suggested_refs: Helena Dragas, in religion the nun Hypomone, arbiter of the 1448 succession

stops.name: Constantinople, a sultan of nineteen
stops.date_confidence: Murad II died 3 February 1451 at Edirne and Mehmed II succeeded at nineteen. Constantine was in Constantinople; the exchange of envoys renewing the peace is attested, and the stop stands where Constantine stood, not at the Ottoman court.
stops.campa: Murad II dies at Edirne on the third of February, and his son takes the throne at nineteen. Envoys go both ways and the peace is renewed with the customary oaths. In the Roman court there is a school of thought that a boy sultan is an opportunity, and men old enough to remember the Ottoman interregnum expect this succession to be contested too. Mehmed has sat on this throne once already, as a child, and was taken off it by his own viziers. He has spent the years since studying how that was done to him.
suggested_refs: The accession of Mehmed II at Edirne, 3 February 1451

stops.name: Rumeli Hisari, the fortress on the narrows
stops.date_confidence: Construction began 15 April 1452 and was complete by August. Constantine is not recorded at the site in person; the protest was carried by an embassy, and this stop stands for that embassy's errand. The November sinking of the Venetian grain ship that refused inspection is attested.
stops.campa: On the narrowest reach of the Bosporus, opposite the fortress his great-grandfather built, Mehmed puts up a second one in four months and mounts guns in it that cover the water. Constantine's ambassadors ride out to the works and are ignored, then insulted, then sent away. He shuts the city gates and holds the Ottoman subjects inside for a day before letting them go, having made a gesture and thought better of it. In November the new guns sink a Venetian grain ship that will not stop for inspection, and the crew that survives is executed.
suggested_refs: Rumeli Hisari, built April to August 1452 opposite Anadolu Hisari to close the Bosporus

stops.name: Constantinople, the cardinal and two hundred archers
stops.date_confidence: attested. Isidore of Kiev arrived with Leonard of Chios and roughly 200 Neapolitan archers. The wider diplomatic network the dossier describes, with embassies to Venice, Genoa, Aragon-Naples and Hungary, could not be corroborated in this pass and is not written into the file; only this arrival is attested.
stops.campa: Cardinal Isidore of Kiev lands in October, a Greek who signed at Florence and came back a Roman cardinal, bringing Leonard of Chios and about two hundred archers hired in Naples. That is the western relief. Two hundred men, against the price of a church. Constantine takes the men, and takes the price with them. Whether he wrote to Venice, Genoa, Naples and Hungary as well, and what came back if he did, is not established by anything that survives.
stops.quote: What did my late lord the emperor not do publicly and privately in his efforts to gain some aid for his house, for the Christians, and for his own life?
stops.quote_source: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus, translated excerpt in 'The Siege of Constantinople in 1453 According to George Sphrantzes,' De Re Militari
suggested_refs: The letter of Leonard of Chios to Pope Nicholas V, 16 August 1453
sources: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (De Re Militari excerpt)

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the union read out
stops.date_confidence: attested. The court reception is described as half-hearted in the account consulted. Gennadios Scholarios had posted his denunciation from monastic retirement rather than delivering it in person.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of December the Union of Florence is proclaimed under the great dome and the pope is commemorated in the liturgy, with the emperor present. The building is nine hundred and nineteen years old and the largest interior anyone in the city has ever stood inside. Constantine has bought two hundred archers with the communion of his own people, and is here to pay for them publicly. Outside, Gennadios Scholarios has nailed up a denunciation from his cell and withdrawn; the monks will not enter a church where a Latin has served. The court attends without enthusiasm.
suggested_refs: The denunciation posted by Gennadios Scholarios against the union liturgy of 12 December 1452

stops.name: The Golden Horn, the chain across the water
stops.date_confidence: The chain is raised on 2 April, the day the Ottoman army encamped outside the city, the Monday after Easter. It held until 22 April, when Mehmed had ships hauled overland behind Galata into the harbour.
stops.campa: The great chain is floated on barrels across the mouth of the harbour, from the city wall to the Genoese tower at Galata, and made fast. It has held every fleet that has ever tried it. On the same day the Ottoman army comes over the horizon and camps outside the land walls. Three weeks later Mehmed puts seventy ships on greased timber and rolls them overland behind Galata, down into the Horn and past the chain. From the twenty-second of April the harbour wall has to be manned as well.
suggested_refs: The boom chain of the Golden Horn, and its bypass by the overland portage of 22 April 1453

stops.name: The Mesoteichion, the emperor takes his post
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the dossier, which conflated two dates: the Ottoman army encamped 2 April, but 'On 5 April, the Sultan himself arrived with his last troops, and the defenders took up their positions.' The siege proper runs 6 April to 29 May. Giustiniani's redeployment to this sector is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Where the Lycus runs under the walls the ground dips, and the Theodosian line has to follow it down; that dip is the Mesoteichion, and every commander for a thousand years has known it is the place. Constantine posts himself there with his Greek troops. Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, the Genoese who has come with seven hundred men and been given the defence, is brought down from the northern gates to stand beside him. Against them, on the far side of the ditch, Mehmed's largest guns are being dug into position.
suggested_refs: The Mesoteichion, the low ground where the Theodosian walls cross the Lycus valley

stops.name: Constantinople, the emperor before the Venetian colony
stops.date_confidence: Barbaro, an eyewitness, records Constantine's address to the Venetian colony; the quoted words are his rendering of reported speech, not a document in Constantine's hand. The address is undated in the excerpt and is placed here at the date of the brigantine's departure, 3 May, which it prompted. The two Barbaro lines used in this file belong to a single speech.
stops.campa: He stands in front of the Venetians of the colony, the bailo Girolamo Minotto and the captains, and tells them plainly that Christendom has left him. Their Signoria is not sending a fleet. He asks them to fit out a fast ship and get it through the straits to find whatever Venetian squadron is in the Aegean and bring it back. Twelve men volunteer to sail her, dressed as Turks and flying Ottoman colours, and on the third of May the brigantine slips out past the enemy fleet in the dark.
stops.quote: Since the whole of Christendom has been unwilling to help me against this faithless Turk, the enemy of Christendom.
stops.quote_source: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli, translated excerpt in 'The Siege of Constantinople in 1453 According to Nicolo Barbaro,' De Re Militari
suggested_refs: The Venetian colony of Constantinople under the bailo Girolamo Minotto, which stayed to fight
sources: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli (De Re Militari excerpt)

stops.name: Constantinople, the brigantine comes back
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged, not resolved. The 23 May return of the single brigantine, whose twelve volunteers voted to come back rather than run for safety, comes from Barbaro's diary via Runciman. The Wikipedia article on the fall says instead that 'a small Venetian fleet of 12 ships, after having searched the Aegean, reached Constantinople on 27 May and reported to the Emperor that no large Venetian relief fleet was on its way.' Two ships, two dates, both in circulation.
stops.campa: Twenty days out, the brigantine has searched the Aegean and found nothing. Her crew put it to a vote in open water: run for Venetian ground and live, or go back into a city that is going to fall and tell the emperor. They vote to go back. On the twenty-third of May they come in through the enemy fleet a second time and report that no relief is coming. Constantine thanks them. There is nothing else in the record about what he says. The twelve of them go back to their posts on the wall.
stops.quote: Captains and nobles of Venice, you see clearly that your Signoria of Venice is not sending a fleet to help me and my unfortunate city, and so it will be a good thing to make ready to send a gripo in the direction of Negropont, to meet your Venetian fleet.
stops.quote_source: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli, translated excerpt, De Re Militari: the order that sent the ship out, from the same address to the Venetian colony
suggested_refs: The twelve Venetian volunteers of the reconnaissance brigantine, out 3 May and back 23 May 1453
sources: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli (De Re Militari excerpt)
Steven Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453

stops.name: Blachernae, the last offer refused
stops.date_confidence: The final surrender demand and its refusal are attested in outline; the exact wording survives only through later authored narrative and no transcript exists. Dated here to 24 May to order the segment; the day is not firmly fixed. The reply commonly quoted from the sixteenth-century Chronicon Maius of Makarios Melissenos is not used. Two lines the dossier assigned to Constantine here, 'the city will take me, dead or alive' and 'The city is all I want, even if it is empty,' are Mehmed II's, via Doukas as rendered by Nicol, and are excluded.
stops.campa: The offer comes in through the envoy: leave the city, keep your life, take the Morea and rule it under the sultan's hand. Constantine sends back a refusal, and the tradition is that he framed it as a decision already taken in common, that they would die of their own free will and not bargain over the place. What he actually said is not recorded by anyone who was in the room, and the famous speech belongs to a chronicle written a century later. Who else stood there, and whether the refusal was his alone to make, nobody now can say.
suggested_refs: The sixteenth-century Chronicon Maius of Makarios Melissenos, source of the celebrated speech that the genuine Sphrantzes does not contain
sources: Donald M. Nicol, 'The Fall of Constantinople,' myriobiblos.gr

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the last vespers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the evening of the twenty-eighth the whole city goes up to the great church, and for one service the quarrel is suspended: Latin clergy and Greek clergy at the same altar, unionists and the monks who have refused them for six months, the Genoese and the Venetians and the emperor. It is the last Christian liturgy celebrated in the building. Constantine takes communion and goes out afterwards to ride the walls. Nobody writes down the hour it ended. The lamps stay lit behind him.
suggested_refs: The vespers of 28 May 1453, the last Christian liturgy in Hagia Sophia

stops.name: Blachernae, the farewell to the household
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The scene of Constantine taking leave of his household and asking forgiveness of everyone present comes principally through Leonard of Chios's letter of 16 August 1453 and its later expansion. The broad pattern is credible and the intimate detail is not verifiable. The Gul Mosque tradition that he prayed at the church of St Theodosia the same night may derive from that church's rose-decked feast falling on the eve of the assault rather than from any recorded visit.
stops.campa: Late that night he comes back to the palace and takes leave of the people who serve him, and asks their forgiveness, one by one, for whatever he has done to any of them. The account is Leonard of Chios's, written in August to the pope, and everyone who has touched it since has elaborated it. Both his wives are dead and there are no children in the room. Then he rides out to the Mesoteichion. Nothing else about that night is recorded by anybody who was in the palace.
suggested_refs: The church of St Theodosia, later the Gul Mosque, where tradition places his prayer on the eve of the assault
sources: Leonard of Chios, letter to Pope Nicholas V, 16 August 1453, via Donald M. Nicol, myriobiblos.gr

stops.name: The Mesoteichion, the last charge
stops.date_confidence: The death on 29 May in this sector is agreed across Sphrantzes, Barbaro, Doukas, Kritovoulos and the Ottoman chroniclers. The charge scene itself is Kritovoulos's, and Kritovoulos was not an eyewitness and wrote for Mehmed in a Thucydidean manner; his own text could not be fetched in this pass and the quotation comes through Nicol's rendering. Doukas separately reports the cry 'Is there no Christian here to take my head from me?', with the same secondhand caveat.
stops.campa: Giustiniani is wounded and carried off the wall, and the Genoese go with him, and the sector opens. Doukas has him crying out for a Christian to take his head from him rather than let a Turk do it. Kritovoulos has him seeing the city gone and going forward into the press with the few still standing. The tradition adds that he pulled off the purple first, so as to be killed as a soldier and not recognized as a prize. No source secures that detail, and the reports of the body afterwards contradict each other on exactly this point.
stops.quote: The city is taken and there is no reason for me to live any longer.
stops.quote_source: Michael Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror, as rendered in Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr
suggested_refs: The Kerkoporta postern of Doukas's account, near tower 96 and the Palace of the Porphyrogenitus, for which modern excavation has found no corresponding gate in the inner wall
sources: Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr

stops.name: The Saint Romanos Gate, the body among the dead
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the exact gate: the identification of the Gate of St Romanos with the modern Topkapi is disputed and the pin is approximate within the Mesoteichion sector. Barbaro reports the hanging story explicitly as what 'was said' in the confusion, not as his own eyewitness claim. Leonard of Chios's account, quoted here, is the one Nicol treats as closest to the event.
stops.campa: By the middle of the morning the emperor cannot be found. Barbaro, who is in the city and writing it down as it happens, records that nobody could learn anything: some said the body had been seen among the corpses, and some said he had hanged himself when the Turks broke in at the San Romano gate. The searchers go through the heaped dead below the wall looking for purple shoes worked with eagles. One report says they found them. Another says the body was never recognized at all.
stops.quote: he was caught up in the melee and fell. He got up, only to fall again, and he was trampled underfoot.
stops.quote_source: Leonard of Chios, letter to Pope Nicholas V, 16 August 1453, as rendered in Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr
suggested_refs: The Gate of St Romanos and the disputed identification of its site within the Mesoteichion
sources: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli (De Re Militari excerpt)
Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr

stops.name: The Golden Gate, the version the conquerors kept
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Tursun Beg and Ibn Kemal describe Constantine fleeing toward the sea or the Golden Gate and being killed there, in one telling by an Ottoman marine who did not know whom he had killed, and beheaded. These accounts are hostile and anti-heroic and are directly at odds with the Greek and Latin charge-and-die traditions. The Yedikule article confirms the site and that the fortress incorporates the original Theodosian Golden Gate towers, but does not narrate the death there.
stops.campa: The Ottoman chroniclers tell it differently, and their version is not built to flatter him. In Tursun Beg and in Ibn Kemal he is running, toward the sea or toward the Golden Gate at the southern end of the walls, when he is cut down by a marine who has no idea whose head he is taking, and takes it anyway. Marble gate, four towers, the arch the triumphs came through for a thousand years. The Greek and Latin accounts put the death a mile north of here, at the Lycus. Nothing in the record decides between them.
stops.quote: On Tuesday May 29 [1453], early in the day, the sultan took possession of our City; in this time of capture my late master and emperor, Lord Constantine, was killed.
stops.quote_source: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus, translated excerpt in 'The Siege of Constantinople in 1453 According to George Sphrantzes,' De Re Militari
suggested_refs: The Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls, incorporated into the later Yedikule fortress
sources: Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr
George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (De Re Militari excerpt)

stops.name: The Golden Gate, the emperor turned to marble
stops.date_confidence: Legend, not biography, and dated to the day of the death only to place it in the sequence. The Marble Emperor tradition develops from the late fifteenth century onward and fuses in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with the Megali Idea. Isidore of Kiev's letter is dated 6 July 1453 or later and is quoted in Nicol's rendering, not from Isidore's Latin.
stops.campa: The people who lose him invent what happened instead. An angel takes him at the instant of the blow and turns him to marble and hides him under the Golden Gate, and there he waits, whole, for the word that will wake him to drive the conqueror out and take the city back. Marmaromenos Vasilias, the Marble King. The story is first written down decades after the fall, and four centuries after that a Greek kingdom builds a national programme on it and sends armies into Anatolia to finish what it promised. Isidore of Kiev had the symmetry it rests on already, that summer, in a letter.
stops.quote: Just as the city was founded by Constantine, son of Helena, so it is now tragically lost by another Constantine, son of Helena.
stops.quote_source: Cardinal Isidore of Kiev, letter of 6 July 1453 or later, as rendered in Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr
suggested_refs: The Marmaromenos Vasilias legend and its nineteenth-century fusion with the Megali Idea
sources: Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr

stops.name: The Gul Mosque, the grave that gets shown
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, dated to the year the Patriarch of Constantinople reported it; day and month not recorded. Coordinates harmonized to the Gul Mosque article's 41.0267, 28.9565; the afterlife lens's pin lay about 800 m southwest. Two rival traditions compete with this one: Evliya Celebi in the seventeenth century placed the grave at the Peribleptos monastery, Ottoman Sulu Manastir in Kocamustafapasa, and a third names Vefa Kilise Camii, the former church of St Theodore, on Nicol's survey alone, since that building's own record does not mention Constantine at all. Nicol's own conclusion is that there is no grave.
stops.campa: Under a pier of the old church of St Theodosia, which has been a mosque since the conquest, they will show you the tomb of the last emperor. The Patriarch reports the belief as general in 1844. Evliya Celebi, two centuries earlier, was equally certain the grave was across town at Sulu Manastir. A third tradition puts it in Vefa. Sphrantzes, the only certain witness to the death, names no burial place at all. Nicol went through the whole of it and concluded that the grave was nowhere to be found, that the body went into a common pit with the rest of the dead, and that the tombs shown to visitors were made by guides who needed one.
suggested_refs: The three competing graves: Gul Camii in Fatih, Sulu Manastir in Kocamustafapasa, and Vefa Kilise Camii
Donald M. Nicol, The Immortal Emperor: The Life and Legend of Constantine Palaiologos, Last Emperor of the Romans (Cambridge University Press, 1992)
sources: Donald M. Nicol, 'The Death of Constantine Palaiologos,' myriobiblos.gr
